note: 0074 and 0077 both named the same residual cell of Nestor#17 and both deliberately left it open: the server-side seam (`memory.add_pair(..., seal_sig=...)`, decision 0077) proves the server can VERIFY a signature it did not sign, but nothing produced that signature outside a Python test fixture standing in for a real client. This decision covers the browser page that actually is that client: WebCrypto Ed25519 key custody in the browser (generate, non-extractable, IndexedDB-persisted; or import an existing raw-hex private key), a read-only `/api/normalize` endpoint so the client can obtain source_norm without blind-signing server bytes, a byte-for-byte JS reproduction of the frozen `signing._message` wire contract (proven against real Chromium via Playwright, not just read), and the 'acting as' box's new third identity mode alongside typed-verifier and shared-key sign-in. Enrollment stays out-of-band and public-only: the page never uploads a private key, only prints the `nestor keys add ... --public <hex>` command an operator runs themselves.

decisions.question: How does the browser get an Ed25519 keypair, and what extractable flag does the private half get?
decisions.commitment: Primary flow: `crypto.subtle.generateKey({name:"Ed25519"}, false, ["sign","verify"])` — extractable=false. WebCrypto applies that flag to the returned PRIVATE key only; the spec (and this Chromium build, measured directly: `privExtractable: false, pubExtractable: true`) always returns the public key with extractable=true regardless of the argument, which is exactly the asymmetry this page needs — the public half must leave the browser (to enroll), the private half must not be able to. The private CryptoKey is then stored, still non-extractable, as a structured-clone value directly in IndexedDB (a documented, standard use of IndexedDB for unexportable key material) keyed by verifier name; `crypto.subtle.exportKey("raw", publicKey)` gives the 32-byte public key as hex for the enrollment command and for display.
decisions.why: Non-extractable is the only setting under which 'the browser holds the key' is a claim about the KEY rather than about the page's source code: an extractable key is one `exportKey` call away from being copyable by any script that ever runs in that origin, which is a materially weaker property and not what #17's threat model (0074) asked for — the operator of the signing instance must not be able to get the key even if they controlled every line of this page. Measured empirically before committing to it (Chromium 1194 loaded over http://127.0.0.1, the actual bind Nestor's `nestor ui` uses by default): generateKey, sign, and IndexedDB structured-clone-store/retrieve of the non-extractable CryptoKey all work, so the property is not aspirational.

decisions.question: A verifier who already has an Ed25519 private key from somewhere else — a prior browser session on another device, a keyring JSON's `private` field being migrated to true client custody — needs to bring it into this page. What form does the import accept, and why not offer both raw and PKCS8?
decisions.commitment: Raw 32-byte hex only — the exact form `nestor.keyring.VerifierKey`/`_ed25519_generate` already use (`Ed25519PrivateKey.private_bytes(Encoding.Raw, PrivateFormat.Raw, NoEncryption())`), so a key already living in a Nestor keyring file's `private` field pastes in unmodified. WebCrypto's `importKey` does not accept `"raw"` as a format for an Ed25519 PRIVATE key at all (measured: `Cannot create a key using the specified key usages` — raw import only works for the public half); the page works around this by prepending the fixed, parameter-free PKCS8 DER header for Ed25519 (`302e020100300506032b657004220420`, 16 bytes, constant because Ed25519 PKCS8 carries no algorithm parameters) to the pasted 32 bytes and importing THAT as `"pkcs8"` — verified byte-for-byte against a real `generateKey`+`exportKey("pkcs8")` round trip in the same Chromium build before relying on it. An optional public-hex field lets the page self-check the pair (sign a random client-side challenge with the imported private key, verify it against the imported public key, both via `crypto.subtle`, entirely client-side) before persisting — catching a copy-paste mismatch instead of silently persisting a key that will only fail at seal time.
decisions.why: Picking one form and documenting the reason (mandated) beats offering both: two accepted encodings for the same 32 bytes is two things to test and two ways for a user to be told 'invalid key' by a page that silently prefers one. Raw hex is what a verifier holding a Nestor-minted key already HAS without a conversion step (the keyring file, `nestor keys add`'s ed25519 branch), so it is the form that makes the migration story (server-side key → true client custody) a copy-paste rather than an OpenSSL invocation. PKCS8 stays an internal implementation detail of `importKey`, not something the operator has to know exists.

decisions.question: The client needs `source_norm` to build the message it signs. Computing it itself would mean re-implementing every `Matcher.normalize` in JS (and staying in sync with every custom matcher a host installs); trusting a server-echoed value would mean blind-signing whatever the server claims the norm is. Which, and what closes the gap?
decisions.commitment: Neither, fully: a new read-only `GET/POST /api/normalize` endpoint (`_normalize` in `nestor/ui.py`) calls exactly the same `matcher.normalize(text)` `memory.add_pair` would use for this domain, writes nothing (no store call, no ledger append), and is exempt from `--read-only` (added to `_NO_DECISION`, tested both ways: allowed under `--read-only`, and a genuinely mutating call stays refused). The page then displays the returned `source_norm` next to the human-approved target and verifier BEFORE signing, in a confirmation dialog the human must accept — so what gets signed is `_message(server_norm, human_target, human_verifier)`, where `target_text` and `verifier` are the exact values the human is looking at (never echoed back from some OTHER server response the human didn't see), and `source_norm` is the one field the client cannot compute alone but also does not have to trust blindly, because it is shown, not hidden.
decisions.why: This is the mandate's explicit threat model (#3 in the task): a client that signs whatever bytes a server response contains is a client that a compromised or buggy server can steer into signing an attacker's chosen (norm, target, verifier) triple with the human never having looked at the actual fields being bound. Showing the norm turns 'the server computed this' into 'the server computed this, and the human confirmed it is what they meant to seal' — the same gap between typing a name and a keyring sign-in that motivates the rest of #17. Read-only-and-exempt-from---read-only is deliberate and mirrors the existing shape of `/api/session`/`/api/session/end` in `_NO_DECISION`: normalizing text is not a decision, and a page that could not compute source_norm under `--read-only` would be unable to even PREVIEW a seal on an audit-only surface, which serves nobody.

decisions.question: `signing._message` is `json.dumps([...], separators=(",",":"), ensure_ascii=False).encode("utf-8")`. `JSON.stringify` is not byte-identical to `json.dumps` in general (control-character escaping conventions, U+2028/U+2029 handling across JSON/JS history, and — the one that actually differs — unpaired UTF-16 surrogates). Which of the mandate's two options (prove-and-restrict vs. reimplement) does the page take?
decisions.commitment: Reimplement: the page does not call `JSON.stringify` for the signed message at all. `pyJsonString`/`pyJsonArray` in `nestor/ui_page.py`'s script hand-encode each string exactly the way CPython's `json.dumps` does for this call's arguments — escape `"`, `\`, and code points below 0x20 (using `\b\t\n\f\r` where Python does, `\u00XX` otherwise), and emit every other code point literally, matching `ensure_ascii=False`. This was verified — not assumed — against live Chromium 1194 and CPython 3.11 side by side, across six cases including a non-ASCII letter, an embedded `\"`, raw control bytes 0x00/0x1f/0x7f, a backslash, and a non-BMP emoji: `pyJsonArray` and `json.dumps(..., separators=(",",":"), ensure_ascii=False)` produced identical strings AND identical UTF-8 bytes (via `TextEncoder`) in every case. The one place the two languages provably cannot agree — an UNPAIRED UTF-16 surrogate in `source_norm`/`target_text`/`verifier`, which Python's `str.encode("utf-8")` refuses outright (`UnicodeEncodeError`, no `surrogatepass`) but `TextEncoder` silently replaces with U+FFFD — is detected client-side (`hasLoneSurrogate`) and refused with a clear message BEFORE any bytes are built or signed, rather than silently producing bytes Python could never have produced from the same string.
decisions.why: 'Prove they agree over the allowed character set and reject the rest' collapses into 'reimplement the encoding' the moment the allowed character set is 'whatever a human can type or paste into a target-text box' — Nestor accepts arbitrary human-authored text as a sealed target, so there was no meaningfully smaller character set to restrict to that wouldn't reject ordinary use. Reimplementing removes the ambiguity entirely rather than trying to characterize it, and the house rule against pinning a constant by importing the thing under test applies here too: the JS is not derived from `json.dumps` (it cannot import Python), so agreement had to be demonstrated by running both and diffing bytes, which is what the six-case check (and now the Playwright E2E test and the extended `tests/test_client_signed_seals.py` vector, both mirroring the same escaping table independently) does. Lone-surrogate rejection is the honest edge rather than a silent one: the alternative (let `TextEncoder` mangle it into U+FFFD and sign those bytes) would produce a signature over text that is not, and never was, the string the human looked at.

decisions.question: Enrollment hands the server a verifier's public key. Does anything on this page's path ever transmit, or even hold in memory a moment longer than necessary, the corresponding private key?
decisions.commitment: No. The page shows the exported public-key hex and the literal command `nestor keys add <verifier> --type ed25519 --public <hex>` for the operator to run themselves, out of band — no network call carries a private key, and no endpoint was added that accepts one (the entire endpoint surface change on the server side is the read-only `/api/normalize`; the write endpoints are unchanged from decision 0077's shape, which already refuses to sign on the caller's behalf). The private `CryptoKey` handle never crosses `postMessage`, never appears in a request body, and for the generate flow never existed outside `crypto.subtle` as raw bytes at all — `exportKey` is called only on the PUBLIC key.
decisions.why: This is 0074's and 0077's own bar, restated for the piece that finally touches a real private key: an instance that signs must not be an instance whose operator can forge as anyone whose key lives there, and the only way to guarantee that is structural, not procedural — a private key that literally cannot be exported (non-extractable) cannot be leaked by this page even if the rest of the page's JavaScript were hostile, which is a stronger property than 'the current code doesn't send it.'

decisions.question: The existing 'acting as' sign-in (`Sessions.open`) checks a TYPED shared key against a value the server holds (`ring.signing_key`, which raises for a public-only ed25519 entry — there is nothing server-side to check a typed secret against). A verifier whose only key lives in the browser can never pass that check. Does the browser-key flow route through `Sessions` at all, and if not, what proves the verifier's identity on a seal?
decisions.commitment: It does not use `Sessions`. `nestor/ui.py` gains `_verifier_for_seal`, used only by `_seal`, `_seal_draft`, `_queue_seal` in place of `_verifier`: when a keyring is installed AND the request carries a non-empty `seal_sig`, the caller's own `verifier` field is trusted directly — no session token required — because the signature itself, checked inside `memory.add_pair` exactly as decision 0077 already specified, is the proof. A request naming a verifier it cannot sign for is refused by the EXISTING seam (`InvalidSealSignatureError`, before any write) whether or not a session existed; a request naming a verifier it CAN sign for needed no session to begin with, because forging that signature requires the private key. Every other write (`unseal`, `restore`, `reject-pair`, `entity/seal`, `reconcile/seal`, …) is untouched and still requires a `Sessions` token when a keyring is installed — this page's browser-key identity can seal through the three endpoints decision 0077 extended and nothing else, and says so in its own copy.
decisions.why: Requiring a session in addition to a valid client signature would not be defense in depth — it would be impossible to satisfy for exactly the verifiers this feature exists to serve (public-only ed25519 entries have no server-held secret to open a session with in the first place, so 0077's own acceptance test — a public-only verifier sealing — could never be reached from the UI without this change), and layering a redundant check around an already-sufficient one is the kind of 'add a condition' fix `docs/agent-guide.md` warns against; the actual fix is recognizing that the two checks were proving the same fact by different means and only one of them can be satisfied here. The narrow scope (three endpoints, not a blanket bypass of `_verifier`) is deliberate: `seal_sig` only exists on the write path 0077 built, so extending the exemption to unseal/reject/restore would require inventing a signature contract for THOSE actions that 0077 never specified and this PR does not either — stated as an open gap, not silently patched over.
